justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space is pushed to the outer edges behind planting strips.
A side path is visible on the right and appears physically separated from traffic by trees and landscaping, which gives some non-motorized users dedicated space.
No clearly visible crosswalk, curb ramp, tactile paving, or pedestrian priority treatment can be identified in the image, limiting accessibility for a broad range of users.
The merge-warning road sign and clear lane markings mainly support drivers, suggesting a somewhat uneven distribution of design attention across user groups.
safety: The roadway is wide, smooth, and clearly marked with lane lines and centerlines, which supports predictable vehicle movement.
Streetlights are installed along the corridor, indicating some provision for visibility and nighttime operation.
The right-side path is buffered from the carriageway by a landscaped strip and trees, reducing direct conflict between fast traffic and non-motorized users.
However, the broad multi-lane geometry may encourage high driving speeds, increasing risk severity for anyone crossing or entering the road.
livability: Dense rows of mature trees and landscaped shrubs create a green corridor that improves environmental quality.
The street appears clean, orderly, and well maintained, with trimmed planting beds and fresh pavement.
There are very few visible people, active storefronts, transit stops, benches, or social destinations, so the corridor feels more like a movement space than a socially vibrant place.
The large road width and limited visible edge activity reduce the sense of everyday street life for all user groups.
sustainability: The extensive tree canopy and continuous landscaped medians/edges contribute to urban greening and potential heat and air-quality benefits.
A separated side path on the right can support low-carbon travel modes such as walking and cycling.
The road design still devotes substantial area to private motor traffic with several wide lanes, which weakens overall transport sustainability.
No bus stop, tram infrastructure, or visible stormwater features such as permeable paving or bioswales can be clearly identified.
aesthetics: The avenue has strong visual order through symmetrical streetlights, consistent lane markings, and continuous planting design.
Mature trees on both sides frame the road and create an attractive boulevard character.
The pavement, curbs, and planting beds appear clean and well maintained, enhancing perceived quality.
Color contrast between green tree canopies, red shrubs, and dark asphalt adds visual richness without appearing cluttered.
comfort: Large roadside trees provide meaningful shade along the side path and sidewalk edges, improving thermal comfort for people outside vehicles.
The asphalt surface is smooth and the roadway appears well maintained, which supports comfortable travel for drivers and cyclists.
Landscaped buffers between the road and side path can reduce some noise and psychological stress for non-motorized users.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or resting amenities, so comfort for people who need to stop or linger is limited.
The very wide open roadway may still feel exposed and speed-dominated for pedestrians and cyclists despite the greenery.
walkability: A pedestrian-accessible side path appears to exist on the right side, separated from moving traffic by a planted verge and trees.
The corridor lacks visible crosswalks, pedestrian refuge islands, or signalized crossings in the image, reducing practical walk connectivity across the road.
The street is very wide, making any crossing potentially long and uncomfortable for pedestrians.
There is little visible frontage activity, seating, or destination density, so the environment is not especially supportive of everyday walking trips.
bikeability: A cyclist is visible on the right-side path, suggesting that cycling is at least possible along the corridor.
Physical separation from the main traffic lanes via landscaping improves subjective safety compared with cycling in mixed fast traffic.
No dedicated painted bike lane, bicycle symbols, or clearly signed cycle priority treatment can be seen on the carriageway or side path.
The high-speed, wide-road character and unclear intersection/crossing support reduce confidence for many cyclists, especially less experienced riders.
